source: Hagger, Chatzisarantis et al. (2016) A multilab preregistered replication of the ego-depletion effect (Registered Replication Report)
finding: Large preregistered multi-lab replication found no ego-depletion effect. Self-control did not run down after a first demanding task.
numbers: 23 labs, N = 2,141. Pooled effect d = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.07, 0.15] (includes zero). Standard sequential-task protocol after Sripada et al.
limits: Only the abstract-level portal record was read this session, not the full paper; no per-lab or moderator numbers. The depleting task (e-crossing) is disputed: Dang 2016 argues it lacks the habit-switching feature of the original (d03).
agent_relevance: Closes the numbers part of gap 6: the d = 0.04 figure is confirmed. A depleting-fuel model of the cost of thinking has no support from the biggest replication. Model cost as a price or opportunity cost, not as a tank level.

source: Vohs, Schmeichel et al. (2021) A multisite preregistered paradigmatic test of the ego-depletion effect, Psychological Science 32(10)
finding: Second, larger preregistered test (two procedures) again found no reliable depletion effect. Only self-reported fatigue moderated it.
numbers: 36 labs, 3,531 tested; 1,068 (30.25%) excluded by preregistered criteria, about 2,463 analysed (Table 4 says 2,461). Confirmatory d = 0.06, 95% CI [-0.02, 0.14], not significant. Bayes factor about 4.4 for the null (abstract: about 4). Exploratory, no exclusions: d = 0.08, significant but small, Bayes analysis not decisive. E-task protocol (20 labs, n = 1,852): duration measure d = 0.15 [0.02, 0.29], depleted people quit about 27 s sooner; composite d = 0.12 [-0.01, 0.24]. Writing-task protocol (16 labs, n = 1,679): d = 0.01 [-0.10, 0.12]. Protocol as moderator b = -0.10 [-0.26, 0.06]. Not moderated by trait self-control, willpower beliefs or action orientation.
limits: Read through a page-fetch summary of the first 100,000 of 147,000 characters; the last third (discussion, supplements) was not read. The small exploratory persistence signal and the fatigue moderator keep a motivational or felt-effort route alive.
agent_relevance: Closes the numbers part of gap 6. Cost of control is better modelled as a felt price that may rise with felt fatigue than as a finite fuel. For the agent: do not build a depleting counter that makes later steps skip thinking; price tokens per step instead.

source: Dang (2016) Commentary: A multilab preregistered replication of the ego-depletion effect, Frontiers in Psychology 7:1155
finding: Argues the Hagger replication used a weak depleting task (e-crossing without the habit-override switch), so its null may reflect a weak manipulation.
numbers: Re-analysis of the replication data pooled across labs, N = 2,058 (one lab dropped for missing manipulation-check items).
limits: A commentary, not a replication. The later Vohs 2021 study (d02) used two procedures and still found d = 0.06, which weakens this objection.
agent_relevance: A boundary condition worth keeping: task choice matters. Not a reason to model thinking cost as fuel.

source: Luo, Du, Bi, Chung, Tang, Yang, Zhang, Wang (2025) Learning from Peers in Reasoning Models (LeaP), arXiv 2505.07787
finding: The 'prefix dominance trap' is a forced-prefix experiment: take the first 15% of tokens of a WRONG response, make the model continue, and accuracy drops by nearly 20 points. It is not a study of models choosing a bad strategy.
numbers: AIME 2024 only. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen (7B, 14B) and QwQ-32B. 32 samples per question; per model 10 incorrect responses from 10 distinct questions that had both correct and incorrect outputs; 16 continuations per prefix at temperature 1. Gap with vs without bad beginning: 19.88 points for R1-Distill-14B. With LeaP peer sharing the 14B gap narrows to 7.81; other LeaP gaps shown are 10.16 and 11.80 (Figure 4).
quote: all selected LRMs exhibit a substantial performance drop of nearly 20% when the first 15% tokens are fixed from incorrect responses
limits: Tiny sample (10 questions per model). Questions were picked because the model had failed on them, so they are harder than average and regression to the mean inflates the drop. The setup cannot separate 'trap' from 'hard question'. Bulut 2026 (d06) finds the same kind of confound in related work.
agent_relevance: Does NOT show that a wrong difficulty or strategy prediction costs 20 points; the MGV citation of 'about 20% loss when models choose suboptimal approaches' overstates it. Gap 5 stays partly open: the cost of a wrong up-front allocation is unmeasured. Still a reminder that a bad early plan is hard to recover from inside the same chain, so S0 should be cheap to redo.

source: Oh and Gobet (2025) Monitor-Generate-Verify, as the citing paper for the prefix dominance number
finding: MGV's introduction cites Luo et al. 2025 for 'nearly 20% degradation when models choose suboptimal approaches'. The cited paper forced bad prefixes rather than letting models choose (see d04).
numbers: Text check of 2511.04341 lines 36-37 against 2505.07787 section 2.1.
limits: Citation drift, not an error in the numbers themselves.
agent_relevance: Corrects the wording of gap 5 and of the evidence for claim K16: treat the 20% figure as a forced-prefix result only.

source: Bulut (2026) It's the Problem, Not the Path: Budget and Difficulty Confounds in LLM Reasoning Trajectories, arXiv 2609.03436
finding: Early-trace signals that seem to predict success mostly read problem difficulty. A pre-registered test found no information in the first tokens beyond a question-only difficulty baseline. Continuing your own prefix beats restarting at matched budget.
numbers: 89 MATH problems x 2 small open models = 178 cells; exactly 1 of 178 is prefix-limited. Continuing beat restarting in 9 of 9 cells where the matched budget fell inside the restart grid. Question-only baseline AUROC 0.83 vs 0.85 with early signals (delta +0.026, CI [-0.054, +0.167]); secondary endpoint 0.88 vs 0.78. Trace-blind difficulty proxy (leave-one-out pass rate) AUROC 0.873 [0.870, 0.876] on 192,315 DeepSeek-R1 generations over 91,573 problems, inside the 0.79-0.95 range of published probes. Within-problem AUROC at t=4 is 0.490 to 0.527 (chance).
limits: Single author, preprint (Sept 2026), small models, MATH only, 16K-token traces. The question-only baseline uses text features and human difficulty level; a pre-generation activation probe could do better (the author says so).
agent_relevance: Direct answer to gap 5 on reliability: difficulty known BEFORE thinking already gets AUROC about 0.83 to 0.88, and adding early thinking signals adds nothing detectable. So an EVC rule should price tasks from the question and from past pass rates, then commit, instead of waiting for early trace cues. It also weakens the prefix-trap story (d04).

source: Brown, Muppidi, Shahout (2026) Predictive Scheduling for Efficient Inference-Time Reasoning in LLMs, arXiv 2602.01237
finding: Pre-run predictors set per-query token budgets. Gains over a uniform budget appear only at tight budgets; at looser budgets prediction errors make the adaptive scheme worse than uniform.
numbers: GSM8K, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, budgets 16 to 256 reasoning tokens. Headline: up to +7.9 points over uniform at identical token cost. Hidden-state MLP, layer 16: test correlation 0.742 with the true success-by-budget curve. Text-only LoRA predictor: Pearson 0.444, MSE 0.0795. 3-way easy/medium/hard classification: LoRA 66.3% vs few-shot o4-mini-high 41.6%; test set 1,294 questions (271 easy, 760 medium, 263 hard), so always answering 'medium' scores about 58.7%. Adaptive beats uniform at 16 to 96 tokens per query and falls below uniform from about 96 to 128.
limits: Very small model, very short budgets, one arithmetic dataset. Equal-cost comparison is against uniform only, not against a random allocator.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 5 on the cost of a wrong prediction: a noisy predictor turns a gain into a loss once budgets are generous. The EVC rule needs a safety margin: when predicted-difficulty confidence is low, use the fixed default, not the adaptive cut.

source: Damani, Shenfeld, Peng, Bobu, Andreas (2024) Learning How Hard to Think: Input-Adaptive Allocation of LM Computation (full text re-read for baselines), arXiv 2410.04707
finding: Allocation is compared with best-of-k at the same AVERAGE sample budget, so the savings are cost-matched against uniform. There is no random-allocation baseline for sampling; random is used only for routing.
numbers: Savings: 25 to 50% less compute for the same success at budgets B >= 8 (math, code); chat: 0 to 10% (full set) and 25 to 40% on the 'tranches' subset (only the queries in the top and bottom 10% by reward variance). Difficulty predictor accuracy, median split: code 74%, math 84%, chat model-routing 72%, chat value-augmented routing 72% (50% = chance). Test loss vs constant-prediction loss: code 0.33 vs 0.58; math 0.48 vs 0.69; chat 0.64 vs 0.67 and 0.55 vs 0.57. Gain at low budgets (B < 8) is marginal. 50% of code problems have zero success probability.
limits: Math and code use an oracle verifier to pick the best sample. The tranches result is selected for high-variance queries and flatters the method. Routing beats random routing but the margin is not tabulated in the text read.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 partly closed: Damani's gain is cost-matched against uniform, so it is more trustworthy than a nominal-budget gain, but it needs a good verifier and shrinks at small budgets. A predictor accuracy of 72 to 84% on a two-class question is the realistic ceiling for pre-thinking difficulty.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally (re-read for how difficulty is estimated), arXiv 2408.03314
finding: The 'about 4x less test-time compute than best-of-N' claim is for low generation budgets and does not count the cost of estimating difficulty.
numbers: MATH, PRM search. Difficulty bins come from 2048 samples per problem (oracle) or from the PRM score (predicted); two-fold cross-validation per bin. 'nearly outperform best-of-N using up to 4x less test-time compute (e.g. 16 versus 64 generations)'. At higher budgets the benefit shrinks with predicted difficulty but stays with oracle bins.
quote: our experiments do not account for this cost largely for simplicity
limits: The paper states the experiments do not account for the difficulty-estimation cost 'largely for simplicity' and leaves the explore-exploit balance for future work. So the 4x is a gross saving.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: the 4x is not cost-matched. For our agent, count the tokens used to estimate difficulty as part of the thinking bill, or reuse them (the estimate can come from the first sample).

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Thinking Economically: Hierarchical Adaptive Budgeter (HAB), full tables (arXiv 2606.01168, Findings of ACL 2026)
finding: HAB's tables compare against other methods and fixed 'step-count' settings, but there is NO ablation that turns the per-step (intra-step) budget off while keeping the per-problem depth prediction. So the claim that per-step beats per-problem budgeting is untested at equal tokens.
numbers: Test sets are small: MATH500 test = 78 questions after filtering (so 82.05% = 64/78 and the CoT 79.49% = 62/78, a 2-question difference); GSM8K test = 462. Table 1 GSM8K, Qwen2.5-7B: CoT 93.94% at 283.0 tokens; HAB 95.24% at 211.1; O1-Pruner 84.63% at 198.7. Llama3.1-8B: CoT 83.16% at 244.5, HAB 87.23% at 232.2. Table 2 MATH500 Qwen2.5-7B: CoT 79.49% at 482.2, HAB 82.05% at 327.3; Llama 46.15% at 572.9 vs HAB 51.28% at 424.8. Fixed-length ablation, Qwen GSM8K: type 0 = 95.02% at 172.6 tokens (cheaper than HAB), type 1 = 95.89% at 310.9, type 2 = 95.45% at 316.3, vs HAB 95.24% at 211.1. MATH500 Qwen: type 0 = 79.21% at 309.5 vs HAB 82.05% at 327.3.
limits: One seed, tiny MATH500 test set (78), baselines retrained with different data filters. The fixed type-0 setting reaches nearly HAB's GSM8K accuracy with 18% fewer tokens, so adaptivity is not clearly paying there.
agent_relevance: Closes the table-extraction part of gap 9 and leaves the question open: no evidence that per-step budgeting beats per-problem budgeting. Do not build per-step token quotas into S0 on this evidence.

source: Jali, Nayak, Joshi (2026) Not All Turns Are Equally Hard: Adaptive Thinking Budgets for Efficient Multi-Turn Reasoning in Agents (TAB), arXiv 2604.05164
finding: A trained budgeter that gives each turn its own thinking budget inside a per-problem cap beats static per-turn budgets and an off-the-shelf LLM-judge budgeter. It is the closest test of within-chain budgeting.
numbers: Budgeter Qwen3-1.7B or 4B trained with GRPO, penalty weight 0.001, on MATH Level-5; solver L1-Qwen3-8B-Exact (math, BFCL) or GPT-5.4-nano (Tau-Bench, Terminal-Bench). Math macro average: TAB at B = 5k matches Static (2048 per turn) and both LLM-Judge baselines with 40% fewer tokens; TAB at B = 8k scores 4.4 points higher while saving 8.5% of total tokens; up to 35% total token savings and 30% latency cut. Agentic benchmarks: up to 20% solver-token savings, up to 15% latency cut after budgeter overhead. Static budgets: 256 to 4096 tokens, or none/low/medium/high.
limits: Values read from text, not figures. Comparison is against uniform-per-turn and a context-unaware judge, not against a per-problem adaptive baseline, so it supports 'budget by turn difficulty' over 'uniform', not over per-problem budgeting. Preprint v3.
agent_relevance: Best available evidence for gap 9: a within-chain allocator beats uniform per-turn budgets at lower cost, and budgeter overhead is counted. For an agent with many tool turns, a cheap per-turn budget (more on planning turns, less on bookkeeping) is plausible; it is still unproven against per-problem allocation.

source: Oladri, Jawahar, Mohamed (2026) Token Budget Saturation and Mechanistic Early-Detection of Reasoning Non-Convergence, arXiv 2607.21433
finding: On easy and medium maths, accuracy is flat from 256 thinking tokens upward, so the knee is at the smallest budget tested. On AIME, accuracy is bimodal: chains that finish are almost always right, chains that do not finish almost never are.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, budget forcing at 256/512/1024/2048/4096 plus uncapped (10,000 ceiling), 200 problems per set (seed 42). GSM8K and MATH-500: minimum sufficient budget (95% of uncapped accuracy) = 256 tokens; uncapped accuracy 0.740 (GSM8K) and 0.625 (MATH-500). AIME 1983-2024: 113 of 200 (56.5%) converged, accuracy 96.5%, mean 4,100 tokens; 87 (43.5%) never closed thinking, accuracy 11.5%, 10,000 tokens. Convergence vs problem number r = 0.431, r2 about 0.186. Hard tercile: converged 100% (n = 18), non-converged 0% (n = 41). Probe predicting non-convergence at token 150: best layer 20, AUC 0.608 +/- 0.080. Fresh rerun: convergence 62.0%, converged accuracy 90.3%.
limits: One 7B distilled model, three maths sets, n = 200 each, preprint under review. Uncapped GSM8K accuracy of 0.74 is low for this task, which hints at answer-extraction or truncation artefacts. 'Difficulty' for AIME is the problem number within a year.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 3 for a different model: the knee sits at the smallest tested budget for easy items, and a cheap rule on hard items is 'stop chains that have not closed by a cap' (about 10,000 tokens spent for 11.5% accuracy). Our own agent's per-bin knee is still unmeasured. Difficulty explains under 19% of who fails to converge, so difficulty-only routing is a weak predictor of wasted chains (supports d06).

source: Kassenaar, Yang, Francois-Lavet (2026) Learning When to Think: Adaptive Reasoning for Test-Time Compute Allocation, arXiv 2608.20256
finding: A 1.5B model learns to pick its own mode (NoThink, Short, Long) as its first token, with no separate router. Cheap modes end up more accurate than Long, so the choice follows difficulty.
numbers: R1-distilled 1.5B, GRPO on MATH, 3 seeds. MATH500: accuracy 0.782 vs base 0.796; mean length 4,796 to 2,811 tokens (-41%). Mode caps: NoThink 1,024, Short 3,000, Long uncapped. GSM8K transfer without retraining: 76% token reduction at higher accuracy than baselines of similar length.
limits: Only the abstract and first page were read. Seed spread not seen. No random-routing control at matched length was seen.
agent_relevance: Evidence that 'choose the thinking mode first' (a cheap S0 decision) can be learned and works. A prompt-only version for our agent needs its own measured test (gap 1 stays open).

source: Bustamante, Lieder, Musslick, Shenhav, Cohen (2021) Learning to overexert cognitive control in a Stroop task, Cogn Affect Behav Neurosci 21:453-471
finding: A misjudged payoff term for control: people who learned that some colours and words paid for the costly colour-naming response kept using it on new combinations where the easy word-reading response was the paid one. They overspent control.
numbers: N = 30 (10 per 'EITHER' frequency group). A higher share of EITHER trials lowered Transfer-phase reward rate (beta = -0.03, SE 0.00, t = -7.30, p < 0.001) and raised goal-inconsistent responses (beta = 0.03, Z = 8.28, p < 0.001). On BOTH trials, goal-inconsistent colour-naming rose with EITHER frequency (beta = 0.03, SE 0.01, Z = 4.38, p < 0.001). The effect persisted despite 40 BOTH trials; participants did improve over the phase (beta = -0.035, Z = -3.55). The LVOC model, a linear feature-based value learner, predicted this.
limits: Very small sample, one lab network (Cohen/Shenhav/Lieder), Princeton subject pool, one task. Confirms the LVOC story but is not an independent test of EVC.
agent_relevance: Closes the 'opened' part of gap 7. Human over-exertion here is a generalisation error: the payoff of effort was predicted from shared features. LLM overthinking (Chen: 1,953% more tokens on '2+3') is a similar generalisation failure, but humans corrected it with experience, whereas an LLM has no in-task correction unless the scaffold adds one. Suggests a cheap 'did the extra step change the answer?' check and a per-task-type cache of whether extra thinking paid off.

source: Estermann and Wattenhofer (2025) Reasoning Effort and Problem Complexity: A Scaling Analysis in LLMs (ICLR 2025 workshop), arXiv 2503.15113
finding: On an unboundedly scalable logic puzzle (Tents), reasoning tokens rise about linearly with problem size for solved puzzles, but for o3-mini they peak near size 100 and then fall. The model spends LESS on the hardest puzzles, the opposite of spending more where the payoff is large.
numbers: Models: o3-mini, DeepSeek-R1, QwQ-32B-Preview, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking. No model solved any puzzle larger than size 100; QwQ failed above 25. o3-mini token peak near size 100; the fall was not seen in the other models. Higher o3-mini effort settings raise slopes and extend the solvable range (up to 10x10 grids) but add tokens on small puzzles.
limits: Workshop paper, one puzzle family, decline seen in one model only, 'frustration' is the authors' guess.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: an LLM can also misjudge the payoff in the other direction (give up early on hard items). With overthinking on easy items, allocation is mis-tuned at both ends. Add a floor on thinking for items judged hard and unsolved, not only a ceiling.

source: Mirzaei (2026) Sample More, Reflect Less: Self-Refine and Reflexion Lose to Repeated Sampling at Equal Token Cost, from 1.5B to 7B, arXiv 2607.28576
finding: At equal measured tokens, no method beat repeated sampling with majority vote, and every method where the model inspects its own output did worse. Extra reflection tokens bought less than extra attempts.
numbers: Qwen2.5 1.5B, 3B, 7B; GSM8K and MATH-500; 150 questions each; 7 methods; 36 paired comparisons with confidence intervals and multiplicity correction. 10 comparisons reliably worse, 2 survive correction; all 18 self-inspection comparisons negative. Self-Refine vs equal-cost sampling: -3.6 (7B, GSM8K, CI [-6.9, -0.9]), -6.3 (7B, MATH-500, CI [-11.1, -2.0]), -4.7 (3B, GSM8K). Forced Reflexion: -5.5 (7B GSM8K), -10.1 (7B MATH-500, CI [-15.0, -5.7]), -9.0 (1.5B MATH-500). Best-of-N with self-pick vs counting the most common answer: 8.0 and 11.3 points worse at 1.5B, 2.0 and 1.3 at 7B (not significant). Reflexion as specified never retried on the smallest model.
limits: Small open models, maths only, 150 questions per set, preprint from one author. No test of agentic or open-ended tasks.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: a forced verification step (self-critique and rewrite) did not repay its token cost here. The 'effort is valued' idea does not carry over to LLM scaffolds on this evidence. Verification that is not independent of the first attempt should be dropped or replaced by another attempt; keep it only where an external check exists.

source: Han, Wang, Fang, Zhao, Ma, Chen (2024/2025) Token-Budget-Aware LLM Reasoning (TALE), arXiv 2412.18547, ACL Findings 2025
finding: A training-free prompt that states a token budget (estimated by the model itself per question) cuts output a lot and scales with difficulty. It tests a stated length, not a stated price or reward.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini, Table 3: average accuracy vanilla CoT 83.75% with 461.25 output tokens; TALE-EP 81.03% with 148.72 tokens (abstract and caption say 80.22% and 138.53, an internal mismatch in the paper). Output tokens CoT vs TALE-EP by set: GSM8K 318.1 vs 77.3 (accuracy 81.35% to 84.46%); MathBench-Arithmetic 313.5 vs 39.6; Middle 553.9 vs 238.1; High 653.2 vs 254.8; College 675.8 vs 259.9 (accuracy 78.00% to 70.00%). 'Token elasticity': a budget that is too small makes the model write more (example: 157 tokens vs 86 for a reasonable budget).
limits: The budget is the model's own estimate, so this is self-pricing, not an external price. No random-budget control at equal tokens. Savings come with accuracy loss on harder sets (-3 to -8 points).
agent_relevance: Gap 1: shows a number in the prompt moves length by difficulty without training (about 40 tokens on arithmetic up to about 260 on college maths). Whether a stated PRICE or REWARD does the same, and whether it beats a random budget at equal total tokens, is untested. Gap 1 stays open.

source: Davidson (2025) AI reasoning effort predicts human decision time in content moderation, arXiv 2508.20262
finding: Reasoning-token count tracks human decision time across items. Items that humans take longer on get longer chains from three frontier reasoning models, and ambiguous pairs get more of both.
numbers: N = 27,071 posts rated by 1,854 Prolific adults. 1 SD more reasoning tokens goes with about 1 s more human time (Grok beta = 1.245, p < 0.001). For identical-slur pairs humans took about 4.5 s longer (about 40% of median decision time) and models used 1.06 SD (o3) to 1.15 SD (Gemini) more tokens.
limits: Correlational; one social-judgement task; item difficulty confounds humans and models. Not an effort-cost choice test.
agent_relevance: Shows LLM thinking length already tracks human-perceived item difficulty, so a model's own length is a usable difficulty signal. Does not answer gap 8.

source: Search record: effort-discounting or demand-selection tasks run on LLMs (2024-2026)
finding: Three separate web searches (extended mode) for COG-ED, demand selection, effort aversion, or effort-reward choice tasks with language models found only human studies, plus work on how LLM use changes human effort and papers on 'discount' in the RL sense.
numbers: 0 relevant LLM studies found. Near misses: Davidson 2025 (d18), Estermann 2025 (d15), and length-penalty RL papers that train a price into the model (RaM, L1, Zhai).
limits: Absence in a limited search is not proof of absence. Search returned titles and summaries only, and the Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs were rate-limited, so no systematic API sweep was possible.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open and looks like a real hole in the literature. We would have to run the COG-ED style choice on our own agent (offer a cheap and an expensive thinking option at several pay levels and fit the indifference points).

source: Search record: prompt-stated price, reward or controllability ('your thinking will not change the result') and LLM thinking length
finding: Searches for a prompt-only manipulation of stated price, stated reward, or stated efficacy found length-budget prompts (TALE, L1, BudgetThinker) and a conceptual 'learned helplessness' analogy paper, but no experiment varying reward and efficacy in the prompt and measuring allocation by difficulty.
numbers: 0 direct studies found for gap 1 (price or reward in the prompt, equal-token comparison) and 0 for gap 2 (efficacy in the prompt).
limits: About four searches only; the efficacy question may be tested in unpublished or industry work.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 2 stay open. They are cheap to test on our agent: same items, three or four prompt framings (no mention, token price, reward for correctness, 'extra thinking will not help'), measure thinking tokens by difficulty bin at the same total tokens against a random-length control.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts Are All Over the Place: On the Underthinking of o1-Like LLMs, arXiv 2501.18585
finding: Reasoning models that switch between thoughts too early are wrong more often: wrong answers carry more thought switches and more tokens. A decoding penalty on thought switching raised accuracy.
numbers: From a search summary (not read in the paper text): wrong responses used 225% more tokens than right ones, with 418% more thought switches; models QwQ-32B-Preview and DeepSeek-R1; sets MATH500, GPQA Diamond, AIME 2024. The abstract page itself gave no numbers.
limits: Numbers come from a search summary and were not confirmed in the paper text.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 comparison: the opposite error to overthinking (tokens spent badly, not too many). Allocation needs both a stop rule and a rule against premature switching. Treat numbers as unverified.
